$schema_note: The 40 TRIZ Inventive Principles with sub-principles and examples. Names/sub-principles from the de-facto-standard English set (Tate & Domb 1997); examples are classic. Original synthesis from this project's vault. For software, read these as a brainstorming checklist AFTER IFR + separation (see concept-software-triz-adaptation), not via the contradiction matrix.

principles.name: Segmentation
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #1 of the 40 Inventive Principles: divide a system into independent or finer parts.

sub_principles.text: Divide an object into independent parts.
Make an object easy to disassemble.
Increase the degree of fragmentation or segmentation.

examples: Replace a mainframe with networked personal computers (a).
Replace solid shades with Venetian blinds (c).

principles.name: Taking Out
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #2 (triz.org variant: "Extraction"): separate out an interfering part/property, or keep only the necessary part.

sub_principles.text: Separate an interfering part or property from an object, or single out the

examples: Locate a noisy compressor outside the building where the compressed air is used.
Use the sound of a barking dog (without the dog) as a burglar alarm.

principles.name: Local Quality
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #3 of the 40 Inventive Principles: make different parts (or regions) non-uniform so each is suited to its role.

sub_principles.text: Change an object's structure (or its environment/influence) from uniform to
Make each part of an object function in the conditions most suitable for its
Make each part fulfill a different and useful function.

examples: Use a temperature, density, or pressure gradient instead of a constant one (a).
Pencil with eraser; hammer with nail-puller (c).

principles.name: Asymmetry
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #4 of the 40 Inventive Principles: break or increase asymmetry in an object's shape.

sub_principles.text: Change the shape of an object from symmetrical to asymmetrical.
If an object is already asymmetrical, increase its degree of asymmetry.

examples: Asymmetrical mixing vessels / asymmetrical vanes improve mixing (cement trucks,
Change circular O-rings to oval or specialized cross-sections to improve

principles.name: Merging
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #5 (triz.org variant: "Consolidation"): bring identical or similar objects/operations together in space or time.

sub_principles.text: Bring closer together (or merge) identical or similar objects; assemble
Make operations contiguous or parallel; bring them together in time.

examples: Thousands of microprocessors in a parallel-processor computer (a).
Link slats together in Venetian or vertical blinds (b).

principles.name: Universality
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #6 of the 40 Inventive Principles: make a part perform multiple functions, eliminating other parts.

sub_principles.text: Make a part or object perform multiple functions; eliminate the need for

examples: The handle of a toothbrush contains toothpaste.
A child's car safety seat converts to a stroller.

principles.name: Nested Doll
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #7 (triz.org variant: "Nesting"): place objects inside one another, or pass one through a cavity in another.

sub_principles.text: Place one object inside another; place each, in turn, inside the next.
Make one part pass through a cavity in the other.

examples: Russian nesting dolls; stacking measuring cups (a).
Extending radio antenna; retractable aircraft landing gear stowed in the

principles.name: Anti-weight
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #8 (triz.org variant: "Counterweight"): compensate an object's weight by merging it with a lifting force or the environment.

sub_principles.text: To compensate for the weight of an object, merge it with other objects that
To compensate for the weight of an object, make it interact with the

examples: Use a helium balloon to support advertising signs (a).
A wing's shape creates lift by altering air density above/below it (b — also

principles.name: Preliminary Anti-action
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #9 (triz.org variant: "Prior Counteraction"): pre-apply an opposing action or stress to neutralize a future harmful effect.

sub_principles.text: If an action has both harmful and useful effects, replace it with
Create beforehand stresses in an object that will oppose known undesirable

examples: Buffer a solution to prevent harm from extremes of pH (a).
Pre-stress rebar before pouring concrete (b).

principles.name: Preliminary Action
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #10 (triz.org variant: "Prior Action"): perform a required change, or pre-position objects, before they are needed.

sub_principles.text: Perform, before it is needed, the required change of an object (fully or
Pre-arrange objects so they can act from the most convenient place without

examples: Pre-pasted wallpaper (a).
Kanban arrangements in a Just-In-Time factory (b).

principles.name: Beforehand Cushioning
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #11 (triz.org variant: "Cushion in Advance"): prepare emergency means in advance to offset a system's low reliability.

sub_principles.text: Prepare emergency means beforehand to compensate for the relatively low

examples: A back-up parachute.
A magnetic strip on photographic film directing the developer to compensate

principles.name: Equipotentiality
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #12 of the 40 Inventive Principles: in a potential field, avoid the need to change an object's position.

sub_principles.text: In a potential field, limit position changes (e.g. change operating

examples: Canal locks move boats between water levels (Panama Canal).
"Skillets" in an auto plant bring tools to the right working height (also

principles.name: The Other Way Round
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #13 (triz.org variant: "Do It in Reverse"): invert the action, fixity, or orientation.

sub_principles.text: Invert the action used to solve the problem (e.g. heat instead of cool).
Make movable parts (or environment) fixed, and fixed parts movable.
Turn the object or process upside down.

examples: To loosen stuck parts, cool the inner part instead of heating the outer (a).
A moving sidewalk with standing people; a treadmill for walking in place (b).

principles.name: Spheroidality – Curvature
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #14 of the 40 Inventive Principles: replace straight lines/flat surfaces with curves, spheres, and rotary motion.

sub_principles.text: Use curvilinear parts instead of rectilinear ones; move from flat to
Use rollers, balls, spirals, domes.
Go from linear to rotary motion; use centrifugal force.

examples: Arches and domes for strength in architecture (a).
Spin clothes to remove water instead of wringing (c).

principles.name: Dynamics
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #15 (triz.org variant: "Dynamicity"): let characteristics change to stay optimal; make rigid things movable/adaptive. Closely tied to the trend of increasing dynamization.

sub_principles.text: Allow (or design) characteristics of an object/environment/process to change
Divide an object into parts capable of moving relative to each other.
If an object or process is rigid or inflexible, make it movable or adaptive.

examples: Adjustable steering wheel, seat, or mirror (a).
A flexible boroscope for examining engines (c).

principles.name: Partial or Excessive Actions
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #16 of the 40 Inventive Principles: if exactly 100% is hard, do slightly less or slightly more.

sub_principles.text: If 100% of an effect is hard to achieve, using "slightly less" or "slightly

examples: Over-spray when painting, then remove the excess (or use a stencil).
Fill, then "top off," when filling a gas tank.

principles.name: Another Dimension
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #17 of the 40 Inventive Principles: move into extra dimensions, multi-story layouts, or another side.

sub_principles.text: Move an object in two- or three-dimensional space.
Use a multi-story arrangement instead of a single-story one.
Tilt or re-orient the object; lay it on its side.
Use "another side" of a given area.

examples: A five-axis cutting tool positioned where needed (a).
A dump truck tilting its bed (c); stacking microelectronic circuits to improve

principles.name: Mechanical Vibration
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #18 of the 40 Inventive Principles: oscillate or vibrate an object, up to resonance and beyond.

sub_principles.text: Cause an object to oscillate or vibrate.
Increase its frequency (even to ultrasonic).
Use the object's resonant frequency.
Use piezoelectric vibrators instead of mechanical ones.
Use combined ultrasonic and electromagnetic field oscillations.

examples: An electric carving knife with vibrating blades (a).
Break up kidney stones with ultrasonic resonance (c); quartz-crystal

principles.name: Periodic Action
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #19 of the 40 Inventive Principles: use periodic or pulsed action instead of continuous.

sub_principles.text: Instead of continuous action, use periodic or pulsating actions.
If an action is already periodic, change its magnitude or frequency.
Use the pauses between impulses to perform a different action.

examples: Replace a continuous siren with a pulsed sound (a).
In CPR, breathe after every few chest compressions (c).

principles.name: Continuity of Useful Action
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #20 of the 40 Inventive Principles: keep all parts working usefully at full load, with no idle time.

sub_principles.text: Carry on work continuously; make all parts of an object work at full load
Eliminate all idle or intermittent actions.

examples: A flywheel stores energy when a vehicle stops so the motor keeps running at
Print during the return stroke of a printer carriage (b).

principles.name: Skipping
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #21 of the 40 Inventive Principles: run a harmful or hazardous stage at high speed to skip its damage.

sub_principles.text: Conduct a process, or certain stages (especially destructive, harmful, or

examples: A high-speed dental drill avoids overheating tissue.
Cut plastic faster than heat can propagate, so it does not deform or melt.

principles.name: Blessing in Disguise
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #22 of the 40 Inventive Principles: turn a harmful factor into a useful one — a core resource move.

sub_principles.text: Use harmful factors (especially of the environment) to achieve a positive
Eliminate a harmful action by combining it with another harmful action.
Amplify a harmful factor until it is no longer harmful.

examples: Use waste heat to generate power (a).
Backfire — use fire to remove fuel ahead of a forest fire (a).

principles.name: Feedback
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #23 of the 40 Inventive Principles: introduce or change feedback to regulate a process.

sub_principles.text: Introduce feedback (referring back, cross-checking) to improve a process or
If feedback is already used, change its magnitude or influence.

examples: Automatic volume control in audio circuits (a).
A thermostat / statistical process control adjusting based on measurement (a).

principles.name: Intermediary
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #24 of the 40 Inventive Principles: use an intermediary carrier or process, possibly removed later.

sub_principles.text: Use an intermediary carrier article or intermediary process.
Merge one object temporarily with another (which can be easily removed).

examples: A carpenter's nailset between hammer and nail (a).
A pot holder to carry hot dishes (a).

principles.name: Self-service
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #25 of the 40 Inventive Principles: make an object serve itself and use its own waste — a route toward ideality.

sub_principles.text: Make an object serve itself by performing auxiliary helpful functions.
Use waste resources, energy, or substances.

examples: A halogen lamp regenerates its filament during use (a).
Animal waste used as fertilizer; using process waste heat (b).

principles.name: Copying
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #26 of the 40 Inventive Principles: use a cheap or optical copy instead of the real, expensive, or fragile object.

sub_principles.text: Instead of an unavailable, expensive, or fragile object, use simpler,
Replace an object or process with optical copies (which can be scaled).
If visible optical copies are used, move to infrared or ultraviolet copies.

examples: Measure a tall object by measuring its photograph or shadow.
Virtual prototypes / simulations in place of physical ones (illustrative).

principles.name: Cheap Short-living Objects
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #27 of the 40 Inventive Principles: replace one expensive object with many cheap ones, trading off some property (e.g. durability).

sub_principles.text: Replace an expensive object with a multiple of inexpensive objects,

examples: Disposable paper cups; disposable diapers.
Single-use razors / surgical masks (illustrative).

principles.name: Mechanics Substitution
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #28 of the 40 Inventive Principles: replace a mechanical means with a sensory or field-based one — closely tied to su-field thinking.

sub_principles.text: Replace a mechanical means with a sensory (optical, acoustic, thermal,
Use electric, magnetic, and electromagnetic fields to interact with the
Change from static to movable fields, from unstructured to structured ones.
Use fields together with field-activated (e.g. ferromagnetic) particles.

examples: Add an odorant to odorless natural gas so leaks are detected by smell (a).
A magnetic stirrer driving fluid via an electromagnetic field (b).

principles.name: Pneumatics and Hydraulics
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #29 of the 40 Inventive Principles: replace solid parts with gas or liquid.

sub_principles.text: Use gas and liquid parts instead of solid ones (inflatable, fluid-filled,

examples: Gel-filled or air-cushion shoe insoles.
Air suspension on vehicles (illustrative).

principles.name: Flexible Shells and Thin Films
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #30 of the 40 Inventive Principles: use flexible shells and thin films instead of 3-D structures, and to isolate from the environment.

sub_principles.text: Use flexible shells and thin films instead of three-dimensional structures.
Isolate the object from its external environment using flexible shells and

examples: A thin-film greenhouse cover instead of a rigid structure (a).
An inflatable cover over a tennis court (a).

principles.name: Porous Materials
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #31 of the 40 Inventive Principles: make an object porous, and use the pores to carry a useful substance.

sub_principles.text: Make an object porous or add porous elements (inserts, coatings).
If an object is already porous, use the pores to introduce a useful

examples: Drill holes in a structure to reduce weight (a).
A porous wick storing and releasing lubricant or coolant in use (b).

principles.name: Color Changes
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #32 of the 40 Inventive Principles: change the color or transparency of an object or its environment.

sub_principles.text: Change the color of an object or its environment.
Change the transparency of an object or its environment.
Use colored additives to observe something hard to see.
If such additives are used, employ luminescent traces or tracer atoms.

examples: A transparent bandage lets a wound be inspected without removal (b).
A red safelight in a photographic darkroom (a).

principles.name: Homogeneity
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #33 of the 40 Inventive Principles: make interacting objects of the same material (or one with identical properties).

sub_principles.text: Make objects interacting with a given object out of the same material (or a

examples: Make the container of an abrasive material from the same abrasive so it isn't
A diamond-tipped tool to machine diamond (illustrative).

principles.name: Discarding and Recovering
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #34 of the 40 Inventive Principles: discard parts once their function is done, or restore consumable parts during operation.

sub_principles.text: Make portions that have served their purpose go away (dissolve, evaporate)
Conversely, restore consumable parts directly during operation.

examples: Rocket booster stages jettisoned after use; a dissolvable medicine capsule (a).
A self-sharpening blade that restores its edge during use (b).

principles.name: Parameter Changes
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #35 of the 40 Inventive Principles: change a physical state, concentration, flexibility, or temperature. The single **most frequently recommended** principle in the Contradiction Matrix.

sub_principles.text: Change an object's physical state (e.g. to gas, liquid, solid).
Change the concentration or consistency.
Change the degree of flexibility.
Change the temperature.

examples: Freeze the liquid centers of filled candies, then dip in chocolate, instead of
Raise temperature past the Curie point to make a ferromagnet paramagnetic (d).

principles.name: Phase Transitions
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #36 of the 40 Inventive Principles: exploit the phenomena occurring *during* a phase change (volume change, latent heat).

sub_principles.text: Use phenomena occurring during phase transitions (volume changes, release or

examples: Use water-to-steam expansion (or freezing expansion) to do work; a heat pump
Expansion of freezing water to split rock (illustrative).

principles.name: Thermal Expansion
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #37 of the 40 Inventive Principles: use thermal expansion/contraction, possibly with multiple materials.

sub_principles.text: Use thermal expansion (or contraction) of materials.
If using thermal expansion, use multiple materials with different expansion

examples: A bimetallic strip in a thermostat converts temperature into movement (b).
Heat a ring to expand it, fit it, then let it shrink onto a shaft (a).

principles.name: Strong Oxidants
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #38 of the 40 Inventive Principles: escalate oxidation along a ladder from ambient air to ozone.

sub_principles.text: Replace common air with oxygen-enriched air.
Replace enriched air with pure oxygen.
Expose air or oxygen to ionizing radiation.
Use ionized oxygen.
Replace ozonized/ionized oxygen with ozone.

examples: Use oxygen (not air) with an acetylene torch for a hotter, cleaner cut.
Ozone treatment of water for disinfection.

principles.name: Inert Atmosphere
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #39 of the 40 Inventive Principles: replace the active environment with an inert one to suppress unwanted interaction.

sub_principles.text: Replace a normal environment with an inert one.
Add neutral parts or inert additives to an object.
Carry out the process in a vacuum.

examples: Fill an incandescent bulb with argon to prevent filament oxidation (a).
Store/handle reactive materials under a nitrogen blanket (a/b).

principles.name: Composite Materials
principles.summary: Inventive Principle #40 of the 40 Inventive Principles: change from uniform materials to composite (multiple) ones.

sub_principles.text: Change from uniform (homogeneous) to composite (multiple) materials.

examples: Carbon-fiber composite aircraft components for a high strength-to-weight ratio.
Fiberglass; composite armor (illustrative).
